title: Posidonius and the tides
hook: a Stoic scientist who studied the tides and the moon

segments.voice: Yesterday: kathēkon, Panaetius's word for the fitting action. Your line was gentler for everyone. Which practice did you make gentler? Day six hundred forty-five.

Stand on a beach long enough and the sea moves without asking you. Water creeps up the sand, then slides away, twice a day, later each day, higher at some times of the month than others. Today an app gives the times. More than two thousand years ago, a philosopher traveled to the far western edge of the known world, to the Atlantic coast of Spain, and spent days watching the water come and go. He wanted to know why. Today: sympatheia.
screen: `THE SEA MOVES WITHOUT ASKING.` → `THE ATLANTIC COAST OF SPAIN.` → `POSIDONIUS WATCHES THE WATER.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Posidonius came from Apamea in Syria, studied under Panaetius, and ran his own Stoic school on the island of Rhodes. Cicero came to hear him lecture. The general Pompey visited him too. He was, by ancient standards, a scientist as much as a philosopher: history, geography, astronomy, weather, all of it. Second, the tides. The geographer Strabo reports that Posidonius stayed at Gades, today's Cádiz, watching the ocean, and connected the rising and falling of the water to the moon: a daily rhythm, a monthly one with the moon's phases, and a yearly one. He didn't have Newton's gravity. But he saw the pattern, and he saw that the sea and the sky were linked. Third, why a Stoic would care. The Stoics taught that the universe is one living whole, its parts bound together. They called that bond sympatheia, a feeling-together. For Posidonius, the moon moving the sea wasn't just a fact about water. It was a sign that the world hangs together, that what happens in one part touches the others. Fourth, what we can take. Studying nature wasn't a hobby beside his philosophy. It was part of it. Paying close attention to the world, the moon, the water, the weather, was a way of seeing the order the Stoics praised. Watching the tides was, for him, a kind of practice. Not everyone today shares his belief in a living cosmos. But anyone can look up and notice the connections.
screen: `FROM SYRIA TO RHODES.` · `AT GADES, WATCHING THE OCEAN.` · `SYMPATHEIA: THE WORLD HANGS TOGETHER.` · `ATTENTION AS A KIND OF PRACTICE.` · then, large: `THE MOON AND TIDES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe in, and out, like a small tide. In, the water comes up the sand. Out, it slides back. Let your breath keep that rhythm for a while. Now picture tonight's sky. Wherever the moon is right now, it's pulling, very gently, at every ocean on earth. It is the same moon Posidonius watched over Gades. You don't have to believe anything about it. Just notice that you belong to a world where far things touch near things. The bell holds the time.
Sympatheia. The Stoic bond tying the whole cosmos together, which Posidonius saw in how the moon moves the sea. Today's word.
Your line: the moon and tides. Tonight, find the moon, if the sky allows, and look at it for one full minute. If it's hidden, look up anyway. Day six hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Historians of science count Posidonius among the ancient students of the tides, and readers of the Stoics see in his work the school's belief that the universe is one connected whole.

original.note: Greek: sympathy, a feeling-together. The Stoic bond tying all parts of the cosmos, which Posidonius saw in the moon and tides.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Stoics were only interested in inner calm.
what it means: Posidonius studied tides, the moon and the earth itself, as part of seeing how the world fits together.
what a scholar hears: Posidonius's works are lost, but Strabo, Cleomedes and Seneca preserve his research, including his tidal observations at Gades and an estimate of the earth's circumference.

notes: Posidonius of Apamea c. 135–51 BC; pupil of Panaetius; school at Rhodes; Cicero heard him (c. 78–77 BC); Pompey visited (Cicero, Tusc. 2.61; Pliny, Natural History 7.112). Confirm.
Tidal observations at Gades and the daily/monthly/annual periods linked to the moon: Strabo 3.5.8–9. Confirm.
'More than two thousand years ago' is safe for the early first century BC.
Sympatheia as a Stoic and especially Posidonian concept: widely held; confirm phrasing.
